opus-5.5.text:
I think this is actually one of the most underestimated problems right now. For a long time, people thought of inference as the "cheap" part: you spend enormous compute on training, and then serving is just an engineering detail. But once you move into the agent era, that assumption breaks.

With a chatbot, a user asks a question, the model answers with a few hundred or a few thousand tokens, and that's it. With an agent, a single task might involve dozens or hundreds of steps: reading files, calling tools, reflecting, retrying, writing code, running it, reading the errors. The context grows very long, and the number of tokens consumed per task can go up by one or two orders of magnitude. And when the agent becomes genuinely useful, people don't use it once a day; they let it run in the background continuously. So the demand curve is not linear at all.

At the same time, model capability keeps pushing in the direction of longer reasoning. Thinking longer really does make the model better, so there's a natural pull toward spending more inference compute per problem. Put those two together, more steps per task and more thinking per step, and you get a kind of compounding pressure on inference infrastructure.

So from my point of view, the challenge has a few layers.

The first is architecture. I think model design must now be inference-aware from the very beginning. Things like how you handle attention for very long contexts, how big the KV cache is, how you use sparsity like MoE so the active parameters stay small: these are no longer optimizations you do afterwards. They decide whether your model can be served economically at agent scale. A model that is slightly smarter but three times more expensive to run may actually lose in the real world.

The second is the systems side: caching, scheduling, prefill-decode separation, making long multi-turn sessions efficient. Agents reuse a lot of context across steps, so if your system can't exploit that, you waste huge amounts of compute.

The third, which I find most interesting, is efficiency in the model's own behavior. Today a lot of agent trajectories are quite wasteful: the model over-thinks easy steps, repeats itself, explores unnecessary paths. Teaching the model to allocate its thinking adaptively, to think hard when it matters and move fast when it doesn't, is in some sense an intelligence problem, not just an engineering problem.

And underneath all of this, of course, is compute supply itself. Chips, power, data centers: these don't scale as fast as demand can. So I don't think anyone will simply buy their way out of this. The teams that win will be the ones that treat cost per unit of useful work as a first-class objective, alongside raw capability. For me, that's where a lot of the real competition will happen in the next couple of years.

r001.rationale: The response predicts sharply rising inference demand from longer agent tasks and reasoning, but does not identify a strong inference cost advantage as a driver of that growth.

r002.rationale: The response mentions KV cache and constrained chip supply, but does not identify memory as a possible bottleneck in inference-chip production capacity.

fable-5.1.text:
Thank you for having me. I think the honest answer is that inference demand is going to grow much faster than most people's intuition, and the reason is structural, not just hype.

When we were in the chat era, one user request meant roughly one forward pass over a few hundred tokens. The demand curve tracked the number of users. But agents change the unit of work. A single task now might involve dozens or hundreds of model calls: planning, tool use, reading results, reflecting, retrying. One user can easily consume a hundred times the tokens they did two years ago, and they're happy to, because the agent is actually finishing something for them rather than just drafting text. So the multiplier is on top of user growth, not instead of it.

And then on the model side, test-time compute is becoming a real lever. We've learned that letting a model think longer, sample more, verify its own work, buys you capability that would otherwise require a much larger model. That's great for the research side, but it means we're deliberately trading inference compute for intelligence. Every step up in capability now has an inference bill attached.

So the challenge, as I see it, has three layers. The first is pure engineering: how do you serve long-context, multi-turn, agentic workloads efficiently? KV cache management becomes central, because agent trajectories share a huge amount of prefix. Speculative decoding, better batching for very uneven request lengths, disaggregating prefill and decode onto different hardware. These are not glamorous, but they're probably worth more than any single algorithmic trick right now.

The second layer is architecture. I don't think dense models at frontier scale are the answer for serving. Sparse architectures, mixture-of-experts, give you a much better ratio of capability to active compute per token. And I think we'll see more work on models that are explicitly designed with the inference budget as a first-class constraint, not something you optimize after training.

The third layer, and the one I find most interesting, is deciding how much thinking a task actually deserves. Right now we're quite wasteful. A model that reasons for ten thousand tokens on a question that needed fifty is burning compute for nothing. Agents need a kind of metacognition: knowing when to stop, when to delegate a sub-task to a smaller model, when a quick answer is good enough. I think the next generation of frameworks will be much more about routing and orchestration across models of different sizes, rather than throwing the biggest model at everything.

If I'm being candid, the constraint over the next couple of years won't be whether we can build smarter models. It will be whether we can afford to run them at the scale people want. That's going to push a lot of research effort that used to go into training toward inference, and I think that's healthy. Efficiency is a capability too.

r001.rationale: The response attributes rising inference demand to agentic workloads and increased test-time compute, but does not identify a strong inference cost advantage as a driver.

r002.rationale: It says KV cache management is central to serving efficiently, but does not identify memory as a possible bottleneck in production capacity for inference chips.

astra-6.text:
I think the challenge is that inference demand grows along two dimensions. More people are using models, but each task can also require much more computation. With an agent, a single user request might lead to repeated reasoning, tool calls, and revisions. So counting requests alone doesn’t tell you how much capacity you need.

And capability changes demand. When a model becomes reliable enough to complete a useful task, people start giving it tasks they wouldn’t have attempted before. That makes demand difficult to forecast.

Meeting that demand requires more than adding hardware. We need to improve inference efficiency and make the agent itself more economical: what context does it actually need, which steps can use a smaller model, and when should it stop? The goal should be to reduce the cost and time required to complete a task successfully. That’s the measure that matters to the user.

r001.rationale: The response describes rising demand from more users, compute-intensive agent tasks, and newly feasible tasks, but does not identify a strong inference cost advantage as a driver of an expected demand explosion.

r002.rationale: The response discusses inference capacity and efficiency but does not mention memory as a possible production-capacity bottleneck for inference chips.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the challenge is that inference demand grows along two dimensions. More people are using models, but each task can also require much more computation. An agent might make several model calls, use tools, check the results, and try again. So the cost of completing a task can grow much faster than the number of users.

We need to improve both model efficiency and the systems serving those models. That includes deciding which steps need a more capable model, reusing computation where possible, and managing latency across the whole workflow. For an interactive agent, being inexpensive isn’t enough if the user has to wait too long.

The useful measure is ultimately the cost and time required to complete a task successfully. As capabilities improve, people will ask models to do more ambitious work. Meeting that demand will require models, inference systems, and agent frameworks to be designed together.

r001.rationale: The response says inference demand grows as more people use models and tasks require more computation. It does not identify a strong inference cost advantage as a driver of an expected demand explosion.

r002.rationale: The response discusses model efficiency and inference systems generally, but does not identify memory as a possible production-capacity bottleneck for inference chips.
